overview: Construction Partners is a vertically integrated civil infrastructure company that builds and maintains roadways, highways, bridges and site work across eight Sunbelt states (Alabama, Florida, Georgia, North Carolina, Oklahoma, South Carolina, Tennessee and Texas). It manufactures hot-mix asphalt (HMA) and mines aggregates largely for internal use, supplying its own paving crews while also selling HMA, aggregates and liquid asphalt cement to third parties. Formed in 2007 as an acquisition platform, the company has grown primarily by rolling up small, local HMA and paving businesses in a highly fragmented industry, expanding from 67 HMA plants in FY2023 to 109 in FY2025 and from 13 to 17 aggregates facilities over the same period.

business_model.summary: Revenue is earned primarily from fixed-price construction/paving contracts with public and private customers, supplemented by third-party sales of HMA, aggregates and liquid asphalt cement. Public-sector work (federal, state DOT, municipal) is the largest and most stable revenue source; growth is heavily inorganic, funded by acquisitions of local asphalt/paving operators.
business_model.customer_type: B2G (state DOTs ~43.4% of FY2025 revenue, no single DOT >10%) and B2B (commercial/residential developers); project-based, not recurring revenue, though contract backlog ($3.4B at Q3 FY2026) provides forward visibility
business_model.geographic_mix: Sunbelt US only: Alabama, Florida, Georgia, North Carolina, Oklahoma, South Carolina, Tennessee, Texas; no international exposure

main_competitors: thousands of local/regional family-owned HMA and paving operators
competitive_position.market_position: One of the largest pure-play HMA paving and construction materials consolidators in the Southeast/Sunbelt; a leading or top-tier state DOT paving contractor in several of its core states, but still a small share of the highly fragmented national asphalt paving market where thousands of local operators compete

moat_factors.description: HMA is costly to haul long distances, so proximity of plants to project sites and aggregates sources creates a natural, hard-to-replicate local cost advantage once a market is established
Owns HMA plants, aggregates mines and liquid asphalt terminals, capturing margin across the supply chain and internally supplying reclaimed asphalt pavement (RAP)

Track record of 54+ acquisitions provides a repeatable playbook for rolling up fragmented local operators and extracting synergies, with access to debt/equity capital that small private competitors lack

moat_factors.factor: Bonding capacity and public contracting track record
moat_factors.description: Scale and balance sheet support surety bonding needed to bid large public contracts, a barrier for smaller competitors
$3.4 billion contract backlog at Q3 FY2026 provides multi-quarter revenue visibility, though backlog can be reduced or cancelled

weaknesses: Thin gross/operating margins (teens gross margin, high-single-digit to low-double-digit operating margin) typical of construction materials industry
No long-term raw material supply contracts; exposed to diesel, liquid asphalt and other commodity cost swings
Growth is heavily debt-funded M&A, raising leverage as the business scales (total debt grew from ~$513M at FY2024-end to ~$1.6-1.8B by FY2025/Q3 FY2026)
Dual-class share structure (SunTx Capital Partners controls ~61% of voting power) limits influence of Class A public shareholders and qualifies the company as a Nasdaq "controlled company"
Customer concentration in state DOT public funding (43.4% of FY2025 revenue) ties results to government budget cycles

growth_drivers: ROAD 2030 strategic plan (announced Oct/Nov 2025): targets more than doubling revenue to over $6 billion and expanding Adjusted EBITDA margin to ~17% (EBITDA >$1 billion) by fiscal 2030

Continued bolt-on and platform acquisitions in a highly fragmented industry (7 acquisitions in FY2026 alone, including Lone Star Paving, Vulcan's Houston assets, P&S Paving, GMJ Paving, Four Star Paving and Ellsworth Construction), expanding into new states (Texas, Oklahoma)
Federal infrastructure funding tailwinds from the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act (IIJA, ~$400B over 5 years) and Inflation Reduction Act, plus state DOT budget growth

Emerging data center / AI infrastructure site-work demand in Texas and Oklahoma (management cites a pipeline exceeding $100 million of data-center-related contract opportunities and believes 70-75% of new US data center construction will occur in its existing footprint)
Margin expansion levers management cites for FY2027: building better/denser local markets, enhancing vertical integration, and increasing operational scale
Record contract backlog ($3.4 billion at Q3 FY2026, up from $2.0 billion a year earlier) supporting forward revenue visibility

business.description: ~65% of FY2025 revenue came from publicly funded projects; reductions in federal (IIJA reauthorization risk, Highway Trust Fund insolvency pressure) or state DOT funding could materially reduce revenue
Fixed unit price and fixed total price contracts expose the company to cost overrun risk if estimates for labor, materials or project conditions prove inaccurate
Outdoor construction activity is highly seasonal and vulnerable to hurricanes, extended rain/cold; management cited unusually wet weather in July 2026 as a margin headwind
Growth strategy depends on successfully identifying, integrating and retaining management/employees of acquired businesses (7+ deals in FY2026); failure to integrate could erode expected synergies

business.risk: Labor shortages and competition for personnel
business.description: Tightening, competitive labor market for skilled crews and management could raise costs or constrain growth
Fragmented competitive landscape with larger, vertically integrated rivals able to bid lower due to plant location, size or scale advantages

financial.description: Total debt roughly tripled from FY2024 ($513.5M) to FY2025 ($1.61B) to fund the Lone Star and other acquisitions, with ~$1.80B of variable-rate debt at Q3 FY2026 (a 1% rate move changes annual interest expense by ~$18M)

Credit Agreements require minimum interest coverage and maximum leverage ratios that step down over time (to 3.75x by FY2027); leverage was 3.10x at FY2025-end, leaving less cushion as the ratio tightens
Goodwill jumped from $231.7M (FY2024) to $943.3M (FY2025) largely from the Lone Star acquisition; adverse business developments could trigger impairment charges
Company flags that instability in banking/financial services could impair access to capital needed for its acquisition-funded growth model

regulatory.description: Subsidiary Wiregrass Construction entered a Clean Water Act consent decree with the EPA (Oct 2025) over quarry discharges; EPA/Alabama DEM filed suit in July 2026 seeking court approval, including a $450,000 civil penalty
Public contracts carry False Claims Act (qui tam) exposure, debarment/suspension risk, and extensive procurement regulation
Stringent federal/state environmental, land use and mine safety (MSHA) regulations govern aggregates and HMA operations and could raise compliance costs or delay permits
Exposure to fines, reputational harm or operational disruption from immigration/employment law violations, including through subcontractors

macro.description: Exposure to diesel fuel and liquid asphalt cement price swings; a newly added risk factor (Q3 FY2026 10-Q) cites the Iran/Strait of Hormuz conflict as a potential driver of crude oil and refined product cost spikes
Heavy reliance on SOFR-based floating-rate term loans and revolver borrowings to fund acquisitions makes interest expense sensitive to rate changes
Rising wages, fuel, concrete and steel costs could compress margins on fixed-price contracts already in backlog
The ~35% privately funded revenue (commercial/residential) is more exposed to a broader economic slowdown than public infrastructure spending

macro_factors.industry_outlook: US highway/road construction and asphalt paving materials industry benefits from non-discretionary, historically stable public infrastructure spending, reinforced by the IIJA (~$400B over 5 years signed Nov 2021) and Inflation Reduction Act funding; industry remains highly fragmented, supporting continued consolidation by larger players like Construction Partners
macro_factors.cyclicality: Moderate - public infrastructure spending (65% of revenue) is relatively non-discretionary and counter-cyclical to some degree, but the ~35% private/commercial and residential portion and overall construction volumes are sensitive to economic cycles, credit conditions and weather
macro_factors.interest_rate_sensitivity: Moderate to high - growth strategy is debt-funded via floating-rate term loans/revolver (~$1.8B variable-rate debt at Q3 FY2026); rising rates directly raise interest expense and could also slow private construction demand or municipal bond-funded projects

guidance.as_of: Preliminary Fiscal 2026 results / Fiscal 2027 outlook release (2026-11-05)

items.notes: Up ~30% from FY2025's $2.812 billion; raised multiple times during FY2026 (from $3.48-3.56B after Q1, to $3.59-3.65B after Q2, to $3.64-3.68B after Q3) on acquisitions and data-center-related demand; figures unaudited and subject to change
Down from 15.1% in FY2025 due to Q4 weather disruption (wet July) and a rapid rise in diesel costs

Implies ~15% growth at the midpoint versus preliminary FY2026 Adjusted EBITDA ($520-524M)
Roughly flat to slightly below the FY2026 preliminary margin; management expects integration of FY2026 acquisitions and completion of lower-margin acquired backlog to weigh on margin before improving
KPI disclosed alongside the FY2027 outlook
Raised from the $165.0-185.0 million initially guided in the FY2025 10-K (for both maintenance and growth capex); figure given as of the Q3 FY2026 10-Q

items.target: Revenue >$6 billion; Adjusted EBITDA margin ~17% (EBITDA >$1 billion)
items.notes: Multi-year plan announced Oct/Nov 2025, assumes normal mid-single-digit annual growth in federal infrastructure investment rather than a step-change funding surge; reaffirmed on the Q2 FY2026 call

guidance.management_commentary: Management attributes FY2026 margin compression to weather and diesel cost spikes late in the year, and expects FY2027 margin to be supported by integrating recent acquisitions, finishing lower-margin backlog acquired with those deals, and passing higher diesel costs through via its contract pass-through/pricing model. Three margin levers cited for the ROAD 2030 plan: building denser local markets, enhancing vertical integration, and increasing operational scale. Management also points to emerging data-center and AI-infrastructure site-work demand in Texas and Oklahoma as incremental upside, estimating 70-75% of new US data center construction will occur within its existing footprint; further upside could come from a recovery in private residential/commercial construction and greater economic/funding certainty.

bull_case: Proven consolidator in a highly fragmented, multi-billion-dollar asphalt paving/HMA industry with thousands of small local operators still available to acquire, giving a long runway for M&A-driven growth
Vertical integration and plant proximity to project sites create a durable local cost/logistics advantage, since HMA cannot be economically hauled long distances
Record $3.4 billion contract backlog plus the ROAD 2030 plan (targeting >$6 billion revenue and ~17% EBITDA margin by FY2030) provide multi-year growth visibility and a clear strategic roadmap
Secular tailwinds from federal/state infrastructure funding (IIJA, state DOT budgets) and an emerging, high-value data-center/AI-infrastructure site-work opportunity in Texas and Oklahoma

New-state expansion (Texas, Oklahoma) via recent large acquisitions (Lone Star Paving, Vulcan's Houston assets, Ellsworth) diversifies revenue and adds scale beyond the original Alabama/Florida/Georgia base
bear_case: Debt-funded acquisition strategy has roughly tripled total debt since FY2024 (to ~$1.6-1.8 billion, mostly floating-rate), increasing interest-rate and refinancing risk as leverage covenants tighten through FY2027
~65% of revenue depends on public infrastructure funding; uncertainty around IIJA reauthorization, Highway Trust Fund solvency and state budget pressures could slow public project awards
Dual-class share structure gives SunTx Capital Partners ~61% voting control, making ROAD a Nasdaq "controlled company" with limited minority shareholder governance protections

Thin, weather-sensitive margins in a capital-intensive, seasonal business - FY2026 Adjusted EBITDA margin guidance was already cut (to ~14.2% from 15.1% in FY2025) due to wet weather and diesel cost spikes

Rapid pace of acquisitions (7+ in FY2026 alone) raises integration risk and goodwill impairment exposure ($943.3 million of goodwill at FY2025-end), while commodity cost volatility (diesel, liquid asphalt, highlighted by a new Strait of Hormuz risk factor) could further pressure near-term profitability
